vibe: Quieter follow-up day after yesterday's OpenAI/Chrome bombshells — today's headline act is a fresh MikroTik router hijack wave plus a cautionary tale about letting an AI agent hold your API key unsupervised.

cyber.title: Attackers hijack MikroTik routers through internet-exposed SSH — no authentication needed
cyber.summary: A live campaign is taking over SSH-exposed MikroTik RouterOS boxes with zero credentials. Lines up with newly disclosed RouterOS bugs patched this week in 6.49.21/7.23.4/7.24.2 — an unauthenticated WebFig file-read flaw and an SSH rekey bug that lets attackers run commands before ever logging in. If you run MikroTik gear, check it's not SSH-exposed to the internet and patch now.

cyber.title: CISA adds seven actively exploited flaws to its KEV catalog
cyber.summary: Two critical SonicWall SMA 1000 bugs (CVSS 10.0 SSRF + 7.8 post-auth RCE), a 9.3 SQL injection in Sangoma Switchvox, and a 9.8 auth-bypass in JFrog Artifactory all made the list this round, alongside Kestra and LiteLLM. Patch any of this gear if you run it — attackers are already using reverse shells and crypto miners on the compromised boxes.

cyber.title: Chrome again exempts Google's own sites from its user site-data controls
cyber.summary: A researcher documents Chrome quietly carving out exceptions for Google's own properties in privacy settings meant to apply evenly to all sites — a recurring pattern that keeps resurfacing every time someone checks.

cyber.title: qBittorrent breaks out of its sandbox — high HN engagement (1,150+ points)
cyber.summary: A widely-discussed writeup on a sandbox-escape weakness in qBittorrent's setup — worth a skim if you run torrent clients on anything you care about isolating.

ai.title: OpenAI says it's hit its "automated research intern" goal
ai.summary: OpenAI claims its models can now meaningfully carry out chunks of AI research independently — echoed in its own "Research Acceleration" post trending on Hacker News (700+ points). Read with the usual grain of salt reserved for self-graded milestones.

ai.title: GPT-6 Astra's developer rollout continues — now showing up on robot arms
ai.summary: Beyond yesterday's safety-card headlines, Astra's developer API is now live and people are already wiring it into physical robot arms — a different angle on the same model, this time about what it can actually do rather than what it's flagged for.

ai.title: "Model fatigue" sets in as AI labs race to ship new versions
ai.summary: A decent temperature check on the current model-release treadmill — Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic all shipping in rapid succession, and the industry starting to ask whether that pace is actually translating to real improvement.

ai.title: Claude can help manage your email inbox, but there are risks involved
ai.summary: A practical look at giving Claude inbox access — useful context given how many people (including you) are now running AI agents with real mailbox permissions.

ai.title: "An Alien Mind" — OpenAI's own essay on AI cognition
ai.summary: OpenAI reflecting on how differently its models "think" compared to humans — philosophical rather than newsy, but decent HN discussion (220+ points) if you want the framing debate.

it.title: "I gave my agent an API key and lost $100. Never again."
it.summary: A relatable cautionary tale about an autonomous agent burning through API spend unsupervised — worth a moment to double-check your own agents' spend guardrails before you learn this one the hard way.

it.title: Cloud in a Bottle: making self-hosting accessible to everyone
it.summary: A new open-source project aiming to make self-hosting your own cloud stack approachable for non-experts, with strong HN traction (585 points) — worth a skim given your side of the fence on cloud vs. self-hosted.

videos.title: Why the FBI Wanted This Hacking Tool
videos.verdict: SKIM — no breaking news here, just a solid evergreen walkthrough of Hak5's Bash Bunny/USB Rubber Ducky pentest hardware and the backstory of why the FBI wanted a dead-simple drag-and-drop version. Worth a skim only if physical pentest tooling interests you.
videos.summary: The host explains the Bash Bunny — a Linux-powered USB attack tool that can pose as a keyboard, flash drive, serial device or gigabit Ethernet adapter to exfiltrate data or pivot onto a target network. Includes the anecdote about the FBI wanting an easier, non-technical version its field agents could deploy without touching code.
